t.textos.lugal-e.version: Sumerian poem of about 730 lines, known from Old Babylonian copies and from Middle Assyrian, Neo-Assyrian and late bilingual Sumerian-Akkadian versions; probably composed in the Neo-Sumerian period (c. 2100 BC)
t.textos.lugal-e.lengua: Sumerian (with interlinear Akkadian translation in the late copies)
t.textos.lugal-e.estructura.0.sinopsis: Praise of Ninurta. His talking weapon, Sharur, informs him that Asag, son of An and Ki, has been born in the mountains, has been chosen king by the plants and the stones, and is attacking the borders of Sumer.
t.textos.lugal-e.estructura.1.sinopsis: Ninurta sets out for war. In the first attack Asag raises a dust storm and Ninurta falls back; Sharur asks Enlil for advice. In the second encounter Ninurta defeats Asag and his army of stones.
t.textos.lugal-e.estructura.2.sinopsis: Ninurta heaps up stones and forms a barrier, the hursag, which holds back the waters of the mountains and directs them to the Tigris, which waters the fields and makes the grain grow. His mother Ninmah visits him, and he gives her the name Ninhursag, "lady of the mountain".
t.textos.lugal-e.estructura.3.sinopsis: Ninurta reviews the stones that fought with Asag or against him: he curses the hostile ones (such as flint and the šu-stone) with humble destinies and blesses the allies (diorite, alabaster, carnelian, lapis lazuli…) with honorable destinies.
t.textos.lugal-e.estructura.4.sinopsis: Ninurta returns to Nippur, celebrated by the gods; the poem closes with his glorification and that of Nisaba, goddess of writing.
t.textos.lugal-e.pasajes.0.texto: Paraphrase. At that time the good waters that came out of the earth did not reach the fields: the icy water of the mountains did not flow down the Tigris, and the famine was great. Ninurta, the lord, piles up stones and builds a mountain of stones like a wall against the enemy land, and makes the waters that were scattering gather and flow toward the Tigris. Now the waters rise onto the fields, the mottled barley, the gardens and the fruit trees grow, and grain is heaped up in the granaries. Then Ninurta judges the stones: to the šu-stone, which rose up against him, he decrees that its body be smashed to pieces and turned to dust; to the diorite, which supported him, he says that it will be brought from the mountains of Magan and carved as a statue of the king for the temple.
t.textos.lugal-e.pasajes.0.fuente: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.6.2 and van Dijk (1983)
t.textos.lugal-e.pasajes.0.nota_academic: The poem combines epic, local cosmogony (the origin of the Tigris irrigation system and of the mountains) and a didactic list of minerals with their uses. The diorite brought from Magan (Oman) is the stone of the statues of Gudea of Lagash, a contemporary of the poem. Asag (Asakku) became in Akkadian the name of a demon of illness. The text was copied for more than 1,500 years and was one of the classics of the scribal school.
t.textos.lugal-e.pasajes.0.lectura_astro: In The Wars of Gods and Men (1985), Sitchin links the judgment of the stones with supposed "Pyramid Wars": Ninurta would have entered the Great Pyramid of Giza, understood as a beacon and control center, and would have removed or destroyed the crystals and stones that made up its equipment.

The poem sets the action in the mountains east of Sumer (the Kur) and on the Tigris; it does not mention Egypt or any building. The stones are specific minerals with the uses Mesopotamian craftsmen gave them (statues, seals, weights, jewelry), and the judgment explains in mythical form why some are precious and others are used for grinding or polishing. The Great Pyramid is a royal tomb of the Egyptian 4th Dynasty (c. 2560 BC).
t.textos.lugal-e.pasajes.0.lectura_actua: The scene of the stone barrier is read today as a myth of hydraulic engineering: the hero tames the mountain waters for agriculture and becomes the archetype of the power that transforms the landscape. The stones, which speak and have a destiny, are a case of the animation of matter that interests the new materialisms.
Synthesis of ecocritical readings; see the introduction to van Dijk (1983)
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.titulo: Inanna and Enki (Inanna and the me)
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.version: Sumerian poem of about 470 lines (partly fragmentary), known from Old Babylonian copies from Nippur
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.estructura.0.sin: Inanna decides to visit Enki in the Apsu of Eridu. Enki orders his vizier Isimud to receive her with butter, cool water, beer and a banquet.
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.estructura.1.sin: Over cups of beer, Enki, drunk, hands over to Inanna in successive batches the me, the divine powers of civilization (about a hundred), swearing each time by his power. Inanna accepts them one by one.
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.estructura.2.sin: Inanna loads the me onto the Boat of Heaven and departs. Enki, now sober, discovers that he has given them away and sends Isimud with various monsters to recover them at seven stages of the journey. Each time, Ninshubur, Inanna's vizier, drives off the pursuers.
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.estructura.3.sin: Inanna arrives at Uruk and unloads the me at the white quay amid the rejoicing of the city; even more me appear than Enki gave her. Enki ends up accepting the situation, and relations are established between Uruk and Eridu.
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.pasajes.0.ref: List of the me (segment I, lines 1–70 of Farber-Flügge's edition, selection)
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.pasajes.0.texto: Paraphrase. Enki, cheered by the beer, says to Inanna: "By my power, by my Apsu! To holy Inanna, my daughter, I will give...". And he hands over to her, in batches of several me, the office of en, kingship, godship, the august crown and the throne of kingship; the noble scepter, the crook and the staff; the descent to the Underworld and the ascent from it; the sword and the mace; the priestess and the lamentation priest; truth; the sexual act and prostitution; the lingua franca and slander; the art of the hero, power, treachery and righteousness; the plundering of cities and lamentation; joy of heart; deceit; the rebellious land; kindness; the craft of the carpenter, the smith, the scribe, the potter, the leatherworker and the weaver; wisdom and attention; the rites of purification; reverent fear and the war cry; judgment and decision. Each time Inanna replies: "I accept them".
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.pasajes.0.fuente: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.3.1 and Farber-Flügge (1973)
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.pasajes.0.nota_a: The me (Sumerian; Akkadian parṣū) are the principles, functions and powers that make civilization possible: offices, rites, crafts, emotions, even vices and misfortunes. The poem presents them as objects that can be given, loaded onto a boat and transported, which has fueled the debate about their nature: things, formulas, insignia? Most specialists understand them as cultural archetypes that exist in the divine sphere. The myth justifies the importance of Uruk over Eridu.
t.textos.inanna-enki-me.pasajes.0.lectur: Sitchin understands the me as portable physical objects containing technical knowledge, comparable to programs or data "chips", which Inanna stole from Enki to transfer technology to her city.

The list mixes crafts, offices and rites with abstract or moral realities such as truth, slander, joy or deceit, which cannot be technical devices. That the me are carried in a boat is a poetic way of expressing the transfer of religious prestige from one city to another, as in the myths of divine journeys (for example, Nanna's journey to Nippur).

Inanna, the young goddess, cunningly obtains from the wise, drunken god the foundations of civilization and carries them to her city: feminist reception has presented her as the figure of a woman who conquers knowledge and power, although the text frames it within a rivalry between cities.
Diane Wolkstein and Samuel Noah Kramer, Inanna, Queen of Heaven and Earth, 1983
